nameStory: This tiny marine creature's name comes from the Greek words 'ptilon' meaning feather and 'hyalos' meaning glass, referring to its delicate, feathery appendages that look almost translucent. The species name 'plumulosus' means 'feathery' in Latin, doubling down on its most distinctive feature. It's like finding a microscopic glass feather duster scuttling around in tide pools!
description: Ptilohyale plumulosus is a tiny marine amphipod, essentially a shrimp-like crustacean that looks like a miniature sideways-flattened bug. These little creatures are typically only 3-8 millimeters long (about the size of a pencil eraser or smaller) and have a distinctive laterally compressed body that gives them their characteristic curved appearance. They're part of the diverse world of amphipods - those small crustaceans you might see hopping around in beach wrack or shallow water. With their feathery antennae and translucent bodies, they're like tiny underwater acrobats.

idTips.label: Feathery antennae
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature is the heavily feathered or plumose antennae that look like tiny bottle brushes under magnification, feeling almost fuzzy if you could touch them

idTips.label: Laterally compressed body
idTips.description: Body is flattened from side to side like it's been gently squeezed, giving it a curved, comma-like profile when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Translucent appearance
idTips.description: Body has a glassy, semi-transparent quality that makes it look almost crystalline, especially when backlit in shallow water

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Very small at 3-8mm long, roughly the size of a grain of rice or smaller, requiring close examination or magnification to see details

idTips.label: Swimming behavior
idTips.description: Moves with quick, jerky motions through the water, often swimming on its side in characteristic amphipod fashion

habitat: This marine amphipod is found in shallow coastal waters, tide pools, and among seaweed beds along New England's rocky shores. Look for them in areas with good water circulation, often hiding among algae, under rocks, or in crevices during low tide. They prefer areas where fresh seawater regularly flows in, particularly around kelp forests and eelgrass beds in the intertidal and shallow subtidal zones.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm up, easier to spot in tide pools during spring tides when more habitat is exposed for exploration.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most abundant and easiest to find, especially during calm days when tide pool water is clear.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper water as coastal storms increase, look in more protected coves and inlets.
seasonality.winter: Much less visible as they seek deeper, more stable water temperatures, though some may still be found in well-protected tide pools on mild days.

funFact: These tiny amphipods can survive being completely dried out for short periods during extreme low tides by curling up in moist crevices and entering a state similar to suspended animation, then springing back to life when the tide returns!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small amphipods, but the heavily feathered antennae are the dead giveaway - think 'bottle brush antennae' and you'll remember this species. Other amphipods have simpler, less ornate antennae that look more like thin threads or have just a few bristles.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertain claim flag**: With only 3 recorded observations in New England, this species may be easily overlooked rather than truly rare, as amphipods require close examination and many beachcombers simply don't look closely enough at these tiny creatures to distinguish between species.
compareHints: Since this appears to be the only Ptilohyale species recorded in New England, compare it with other hyalid amphipods by focusing on those distinctive feathery antennae - they're much more elaborate than the simpler antennae of related species. Other small amphipods in the family tend to have thread-like or lightly bristled antennae rather than the ornate, plume-like structures that make this species special.
